title: Catalan Numbers
directAnswer: The nth Catalan number Cₙ counts a surprising number of things: distinct BSTs with n nodes, valid sequences of n balanced parenthesis pairs, full binary trees with n+1 leaves, and triangulations of a polygon. Two ways to compute it. DP: C₀ = 1 and Cₙ = Σ (Cᵢ · Cₙ₋₁₋ᵢ) for i = 0..n−1, in O(n²) — the split recurrence that mirrors choosing a root. Closed form: Cₙ = C(2n, n) / (n + 1), in O(n) — one central binomial coefficient divided by n+1. Under a prime modulus, the division becomes multiply-by-modular-inverse.

remember.pattern: Catalan = split-point DP recurrence, or central binomial C(2n,n)/(n+1)
remember.formula:
DP:  C[0] = 1;  C[n] = sum over i in [0, n-1] of C[i] * C[n-1-i]
Closed form:  C(n) = C(2n, n) / (n + 1)
Mod p (prime):  C(n) = C(2n, n) * inverse(n + 1) mod p
rules: The DP recurrence splits on the **root / first matched pair**: `Cₙ = Σ Cᵢ · Cₙ₋₁₋ᵢ`. The two indices must sum to `n − 1` (the remaining items after fixing one), not `n` — the off-by-one trap.
Closed form `C(2n,n)/(n+1)` divides exactly over the integers, but under a prime mod you must multiply by the **modular inverse** of `n+1`, never integer-divide.
Catalan numbers grow like `4ⁿ / (n^1.5 √π)` — `C₃₅` already overflows a 64-bit integer, so use `long` carefully or compute mod p / with big integers.
DP is `O(n²)`; the closed form is `O(n)`. Prefer the formula when you only need a single `Cₙ`, the DP when you also want all of `C₀..Cₙ`.
Base case `C₀ = 1` (the empty structure: one empty tree, one empty parenthesis string) — forgetting it zeroes the whole table.
whenToUse: Counting **distinct BSTs / full binary trees** with n nodes (LeetCode 96)
Counting **valid balanced-parenthesis** sequences of n pairs (LeetCode 22 counts them)
Counting polygon triangulations, monotonic lattice paths under the diagonal, or stack-sortable permutations
Any recurrence of the shape 'pick a split point, multiply the two independent sub-counts, sum over splits'
antiSignals: You must **enumerate** the structures, not count them → backtracking, not a Catalan formula
The objects aren't independent across the split → the product form Cᵢ·Cₙ₋₁₋ᵢ doesn't apply
n is tiny and one-off → just look up or hardcode the small Catalan values
You need it mod a **composite** → Fermat's inverse of n+1 fails; use extended-GCD inverse
remember.takeaway: Catalan numbers are the answer whenever a count decomposes as 'fix one element, then the left and right parts are independent and each is a smaller instance of the same count'. That split gives the O(n²) convolution DP; the closed form C(2n,n)/(n+1) collapses it to O(n). The recurring traps are the n−1 index in the split and treating the closed-form division as integer division under a modulus.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognise the Catalan structure behind 'count the BSTs / balanced parens', can write the split-point convolution recurrence with the correct n−1 indexing, and know the closed form plus how to handle its division under a modulus.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Indexing the split as Cᵢ·Cₙ₋ᵢ (sums to n, off by one) instead of Cᵢ·Cₙ₋₁₋ᵢ, or integer-dividing C(2n,n) by (n+1) under a prime mod instead of multiplying by the inverse.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Explain WHY the recurrence is a convolution — fixing the root (or the first matched pair) splits the remaining n−1 items into independent left/right sub-instances — and mention the closed form turns O(n²) into O(n).

problemStatement:
Compute the nth **Catalan number** `Cₙ`.

The Catalan numbers begin `1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, 132, …` and count, among many things: the number of distinct binary search trees with `n` nodes, the number of valid sequences of `n` pairs of balanced parentheses, and the number of triangulations of a convex `(n + 2)`-gon.

Return `Cₙ` exactly (for small `n`) or modulo a given prime `p` (for large `n`).
constraints: 0 ≤ n ≤ 10⁶ when working modulo a prime p
0 ≤ n ≤ 33 if returning an exact 64-bit value (C₃₅ overflows a signed 64-bit integer)
p is prime and p > 2n when using the closed form mod p (so inverses exist)
understanding: Catalan numbers count structures that decompose recursively into two independent smaller structures. Take BSTs with n nodes: choose which value is the root (n choices), and then the left subtree is a BST on the i smaller values and the right is a BST on the n−1−i larger values — independent, and each a smaller Catalan count. Summing the product over all root choices gives the recurrence. The same split — first matched parenthesis pair, root of a triangulation fan — explains every Catalan interpretation. The closed form is a counting shortcut for the same quantity.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do you want a single Cₙ, or all of C₀..Cₙ?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: If just one, the closed form C(2n,n)/(n+1) is O(n). If I need the whole table (common when it's a subproblem), the DP recurrence gives all of them in O(n²).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Exact value or modulo a prime?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Catalan grows like 4ⁿ, so beyond n ≈ 33 it overflows 64 bits. For large n we work modulo a prime p and replace the division by n+1 with a modular inverse.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the modulus prime, and is p > 2n?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: I'll assume prime p > 2n so Fermat's inverse of (n+1) and of the factorials all exist. A composite modulus would need extended-GCD inverses.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What's C₀?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: 1 — the empty tree / empty parenthesis string. It's the base case; dropping it zeroes the recurrence.

examples.explanation: 5 BSTs with 3 nodes; 5 valid 3-pair parenthesis strings: ((())), (()()), (())(), ()(()), ()()().
C₄ = C(8,4)/5 = 70/5 = 14. The DP sum C₀C₃+C₁C₂+C₂C₁+C₃C₀ = 5+2+2+5 = 14 agrees.
One empty structure. Base case C₀ = 1.

approaches.name: Convolution DP (Baseline / All Values)
approaches.whenToMention: Mention first — it makes the recursive split explicit and gives every C₀..Cₙ, which the interviewer often actually wants.
hints: Think about counting BSTs with n nodes. If you fix which value is the root, what are the left and right subtrees, and are they independent?
Root choice i splits the rest into a left subtree of i nodes and a right subtree of n−1−i nodes. Both are smaller Catalan counts, and they're chosen independently — so their counts multiply.
Sum that product over every root choice: C[n] = Σ C[i]·C[n−1−i] for i = 0..n−1, with C[0] = 1. Build the table from small n upward.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Computing C[n] sums n products, and we do this for each n up to the target, giving 1 + 2 + … + n ≈ n²/2 = O(n²) multiplications. The table of Catalan values is O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Build the Catalan values bottom-up from the split recurrence. Set `C[0] = 1`, then for each `n` compute `C[n] = Σ_{i=0}^{n−1} C[i]·C[n−1−i]`.

**Where the recurrence comes from.** Count BSTs with `n` nodes (values `1..n`). Fix the root to be the `(i+1)`-th smallest value. Then the `i` values below it form the left subtree and the `n−1−i` values above it form the right subtree. Crucially, the shape of the left subtree and the shape of the right subtree are chosen **independently**, and each is itself a Catalan count on fewer nodes — `C[i]` and `C[n−1−i]`. Independence means the number of combined trees for this root is the **product** `C[i]·C[n−1−i]`. Summing over all `n` root choices gives the recurrence. The identical split explains balanced parentheses (fix the partner of the first `(`: it encloses `i` pairs, leaving `n−1−i` pairs after it) and polygon triangulations.

**Why the indices sum to n−1, not n.** Fixing the root consumes one node, so only `n−1` remain to distribute between the two subtrees. That's why the second index is `n−1−i`. Writing `C[i]·C[n−i]` (summing to `n`) double-counts and is the single most common bug here.

**Why bottom-up.** Each `C[n]` depends only on smaller indices, so filling the table in increasing `n` means every term on the right is already known. No recursion stack, no recomputation.

**Cost and overflow.** Computing `C[n]` does `n` multiplications, so the whole table is `O(n²)`. Catalan values explode like `4ⁿ`, so for exact values beyond `n ≈ 33` you must work modulo a prime (reduce after each multiply, `long` in Java) or use big integers in Python.
approaches.insight: The DP is the honest expression of the structure: 'fix one element, multiply the independent sub-counts, sum over choices.' It's the right tool when you need every C₀..Cₙ (e.g. as a subroutine). Its only weakness is the O(n²) convolution — which the closed form removes when you need just one value.

dryRun.intro: Fill C[0..4] bottom-up; each C[n] convolves the known prefix with its reverse. Indices in each product sum to n−1.

java.explanation: Base case: one empty structure. Omit it and the whole table is zero.
The convolution: left part i nodes, right part k−1−i nodes — indices MUST sum to k−1.
Modular variant: reduce after every addition so the long never overflows.

python.line: c[k] = sum(c[i] * c[k - 1 - i] for i in range(k))
python.explanation: Convolution over splits; Python big ints hold exact values for any n.
Modular accumulation for large n under prime p.

diagrams.title: Catalan DP table filling up
diagrams.caption: Each new cell convolves the known prefix with its reverse; highlighted cell is the one just computed.

pitfalls: Indices summing to k instead of k−1 — the off-by-one that breaks the count.
Forgetting C[0] = 1 — zeroes the entire table.
Letting the exact value overflow for n > 33 — switch to mod p or big integers.
Recomputing recursively without memoisation — exponential blowup.

approaches.name: Closed Form C(2n,n)/(n+1) (Optimal Single Value)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want for a single large Cₙ. Phrase it as 'central binomial over n+1, with the division done by modular inverse under a prime'.

complexity.space: O(n) for factorial tables (O(1) for exact small n)

hints: There's a closed form: Cₙ = C(2n, n) / (n + 1). It divides exactly over the integers. How do you compute a single C(2n, n) efficiently?
Precompute factorials and their modular inverses up to 2n, then C(2n, n) = fact[2n]·invFact[n]·invFact[n] mod p.
The /(n+1) is a division — under a prime mod, multiply by the modular inverse of (n+1) via Fermat: (n+1)^(p−2) mod p. Never integer-divide modulo p.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Building factorial and inverse-factorial tables up to 2n is O(n) (one Fermat inverse plus a backward sweep). After that, each Catalan number is a constant number of multiplications, so O(1) per value. Tables are O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Use the identity `Cₙ = C(2n, n) / (n + 1)`, where `C(2n, n)` is the central binomial coefficient.

**Why the formula holds (sketch).** `C(2n, n)` counts all lattice paths from `(0,0)` to `(n,n)` using unit right/up steps. The Catalan number counts only those that never cross above the diagonal. André's reflection argument shows the 'bad' paths are in bijection with `C(2n, n+1)` of them, and `C(2n,n) − C(2n,n+1) = C(2n,n)/(n+1)`. The upshot: the central binomial, divided by `n+1`, is exactly `Cₙ` — and the division is always exact over the integers.

**Computing it exactly for small n.** Multiply `C(2n, n)` with a running product (dividing as you go to keep numbers small) and divide once by `n+1`. Fine while `Cₙ` fits in 64 bits (`n ≤ 33`).

**Computing it modulo a prime for large n.** Two changes. First, `C(2n, n) = fact[2n] · invFact[n] · invFact[n] mod p`, using precomputed factorials and Fermat inverse-factorials (one modpow plus a backward sweep, exactly as in nCr mod p). Second — the trap — the `/(n+1)` **cannot** be integer division under a modulus. Replace it with multiplication by the modular inverse of `n+1`: since `p` is prime and `p > n+1`, `(n+1)⁻¹ ≡ (n+1)^(p−2) (mod p)` by Fermat. So `Cₙ ≡ C(2n,n) · (n+1)^(p−2) (mod p)`.

**Why p > 2n matters.** The factorial `fact[2n]` must not contain a factor of `p`, or it would be `0 mod p` and have no inverse. Requiring `p > 2n` guarantees that and keeps every inverse well-defined.

**Overflow safety.** All modular products are of two values below `p ≈ 10⁹`, so each fits in a 64-bit `long` provided you reduce `mod p` after every multiplication. Python integers are unbounded; the modulus there is for matching the math and for speed.
approaches.insight: The closed form trades the O(n²) convolution for O(n) factorial precompute and O(1) per value — the right move when you need a single large Cₙ. The two things to get right: it's C(2n,n) over (n+1), and under a modulus that division is a multiply-by-inverse. It reuses the exact factorial/inverse machinery from nCr mod p, so Catalan is essentially a one-line wrapper around binomial coefficients.

dryRun.intro: Closed form Cₙ = C(2n,n)/(n+1). Compute C(8,4), then divide by 5.

steps.action: if computing mod p, replace /5 with ·5⁻¹ (Fermat)

java.explanation: Builds C(2n,n) dividing as it goes so intermediate stays small; 2L*n forces long to avoid int overflow.
Exact integer division — valid ONLY because we're not working mod p here.

java.line: long central = fact[2 * n] * invFact[n] % p * invFact[n] % p;
java.explanation: C(2n,n) mod p via factorial tables; mod between products keeps the long < p².
Fermat inverse of n+1 — this is what replaces the division under a modulus.
Multiply by the inverse instead of dividing — the key correctness point mod p.

python.explanation: Central binomial with running exact division; big ints mean no overflow.
Exact division for the non-modular path.
Built-in modular inverse via Fermat for the modular path.
Catalan mod p = C(2n,n)·(n+1)⁻¹ — multiply, don't divide.

diagrams.caption: Cₙ = C(2n,n)/(n+1). Row shows n, C(2n,n), and the resulting Catalan number.

pitfalls: Integer-dividing C(2n,n) by (n+1) under a modulus — must multiply by the inverse.
Using fact[2n] when p ≤ 2n — fact[2n] is 0 mod p and has no inverse; require p > 2n.
Multiplying out C(2n,n) without divide-as-you-go in the exact path — overflows sooner.
Forgetting that the exact path only survives to n ≈ 33 before 64-bit overflow.

edgeCases.behavior: C(0,0)/1 = 1; the loop runs zero times and result/1 = 1.
Uses factorial tables and Fermat inverse of n+1; needs p prime and p > 2n.

commonMistakes: Writing the recurrence with indices summing to n instead of n−1.
Integer-dividing C(2n,n) by (n+1) when working modulo a prime instead of multiplying by the inverse.
Letting exact Catalan values overflow 64 bits for n > 33.
Using the closed form mod p when p ≤ 2n, so fact[2n] has no inverse.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Off-by-one in the split recurrence
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Fixing the root uses one node, leaving n−1 to split. The product must be Cᵢ·Cₙ₋₁₋ᵢ (indices sum to n−1). Using Cᵢ·Cₙ₋ᵢ over-counts and gives wrong values from C₂ onward.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Dividing by (n+1) under a modulus
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Modular arithmetic has no division. C(2n,n)/(n+1) mod p must become C(2n,n)·(n+1)⁻¹ mod p, with the inverse from Fermat. Integer division gives a wrong residue.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
central = fact[2 * n] * inv_fact[n] % p * inv_fact[n] % p
return central // (n + 1) % p   # WRONG under a modulus
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
central = fact[2 * n] * inv_fact[n] % p * inv_fact[n] % p
return central * pow(n + 1, p - 2, p) % p  # multiply by inverse

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Exact value overflow for large n
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Catalan numbers grow like 4ⁿ; C₃₅ exceeds a signed 64-bit integer. Computing exactly with long silently overflows to garbage.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: long c = catalanClosed(40); // overflows long — wrong
commonMistakesDetailed.good: long c = catalanMod(40, 1_000_000_007L, fact, invFact); // work mod p

followupVariations.title: Unique Binary Search Trees
followupVariations.hint: The count of BSTs with n nodes IS Cₙ — the convolution DP is the intended solution.

followupVariations.title: Generate Parentheses
followupVariations.hint: The number of valid n-pair strings is Cₙ; generating them is backtracking, counting them is Catalan.

followupVariations.title: nCr mod p
followupVariations.hint: The closed form is just a central binomial coefficient over n+1 — reuses factorial/inverse tables.

followupVariations.title: Lucas' Theorem
followupVariations.hint: If you need Catalan mod a small prime with large n, compute C(2n,n) mod p via Lucas.

patternNote: Catalan / convolution counting. Recognise it whenever a count decomposes as 'fix one element, the left and right parts are independent smaller instances'. The O(n²) split DP gives all values; the O(n) closed form C(2n,n)/(n+1) gives one. Shows up in BST counts, balanced parentheses, triangulations, and stack-sortable permutations.
